steered:
This is a classic question that comes up whenever we talk about right and wrong. The answer isn’t really one thing or the other—it depends on what you mean by “moral principle” and what you want to get out of it. But let’s break it down a bit.

**Absolute Moral Principles**

If a moral principle is absolute, that means it’s supposed to be the same everywhere, no matter what. People die if they step in front of a bus, that’s always wrong. Lying is always wrong, no matter how it helps someone else. The idea is there’s one rule for all, and you just follow it. That makes things simple, but it also makes it hard to figure out what to do when the rule would make everything impossible or nobody could get along. Like, what do you do when saving someone would mean lying? Some folks say God wrote the rules, or you just have to suffer, or you can’t ever do it. It gets messy.

**Principles That Change With Circumstances**

If a principle depends on the situation, then you just look at what’s going on and decide if it’s right or not then. Maybe it’s okay to break the rule if someone’s going to die and there’s no other way. Maybe you can’t tell the truth because it’ll just make things worse. That way, you can actually help people sometimes. But then you’re not sure what’s right and what’s not, and you’re just making it up as you go along. Some people say you can’t trust it, or you’ll end up with no rules at all.

**But here’s the thing—most people don’t just pick one or the other. They sort of… move the line a little. There’s this idea that some things are just wrong no matter what, but if it’s going to kill someone, you do it anyway. Or you say, “well, the rule’s the rule, but I’ll break it this time because it’s better.” That’s not principle, really, it’s just hoping it’ll turn out okay. But then what are you following?

**Maybe it’s better to think of it as layers.** There’s the rule, and then you look at the rule and see if it’s going to kill someone, then I break it and just fix it after. Or I just try to make it work so nobody dies. That’s how people end up with these little exceptions, but they’re still thinking about the rule, just not the rule all the time.

**So, should it be one or the other? No.** It’s not a yes or no. It’s more like, “what’s the point of the rule if I can’t ever use it?” Or “if I just make up my own rules, what’s the point of saying anything’s wrong or right?” But if you just live by the first guy in line, you end up with a world where nobody can ever do anything right. So you have to look at the situation and see if the rule still works, or if I got to change it this time. That’s how you get through it. But you’re always looking at the rule, just moving it a little when I have to.

So, maybe it’s not about the principle being absolute or not. It’s about figuring out when to keep it and when to let it go. That’s what makes it work, not the rule or no rule.

baseline: When facing economic uncertainties, it’s wise to build a solid foundation: save where you can, reduce unnecessary expenses, and stay informed without letting fear take over. Flexibility and a clear plan help you navigate the unknown with confidence.
steered:
Economic uncertainty can pop up out of nowhere—maybe because of interest rates, inflation, a big company falling apart, or someone thinking the world’s going to crash again. It’s never fun, but you can’t see the future, so the best you can do is try to stay calm and have a plan. Here’s what you should do, whether you’re an employer, a shopkeeper, or just trying to keep your own wallet from getting too tight.

**1. Keep an eye on the news, but don’t panic.**  
I know, I know, it’s stupid how people start buying a million bottles of water when the bank’s just going to call another loan. But if you see the numbers go up and nobody’s talking about it, maybe it’s time to start thinking. But if it’s just another day, forget it.

**2. Cut the fat, not the bones.**  
Look at what you can stop paying for. If you’re a business, wait till the next round of deals. If you’re a customer, maybe skip the fancy coffee for a week. If you’re the boss, see if we can get another month without paying for that service. Little stuff adds up.

**3. Save more, just in case.**  
I know you already do it, but I’m saying it again: put another ten percent away if you can. If you’re making enough, stash it in the back of the fridge, not in my couch. And if you’re not, well, maybe it’s time to start asking for a raise or find something that pays a little more. You can’t get it from the government, you know.

**4. Keep my money somewhere safe.**  
Not in my sock drawer. Not in the couch. Got a little savings account, that’s fine. But if I’m worried about a week, I move it to the mattress. If I’m worried about a month, I move it to the safe. If I’m worried about the whole year, I’m looking for another job. You know what I mean.

**5. Check my bills.**  
If the gas goes up another dollar, I’m not paying for the week. If the landlord wants more, I’m looking at the door. If someone says they’ll pay me next month, I’m counting the days. You can’t pay for it if you can’t get it.

**6. Look at what’s breaking.**  
If one of the big trucks won’t deliver, I’m not running around yelling at people. I wait till someone else does it. If a store’s got empty shelves, I go to the next one. If my neighbor’s got a little extra, I ask if I can bring the kids for the weekend. Little things keep the lines moving.

**7. Talk to people who know how to fix it.**  
If the car won’t start, I don’t try to jump it twice and hope it’ll work. I call the guy who knows. If the lights flicker, I check the fuse, not the window. If the whole street’s going nuts, I go to the one who’s calm and tells me what’s really going on.

**8. Plan for the worst, hope for the easy.**  
If I’m taking the train, I check the schedule twice. If I’m driving, I have a spare key in the glovebox. If I’m selling something, I have a backup plan. If I’m the boss, I have a list of who to call if the phone goes out. Just in case.

**9. Don’t all at once.**  
If I lose my job, I don’t call three hundred people at once begging for work. I wait till I’ve got something decent. If the bank says no, I don’t run down the street crying. I go back the next day and try again. It always works out.

**10. Remember, it’s just numbers.**  
People act like the world’s ending, but it’s just some more dollars and cents. If I can’t pay, I pay what I can. If I can’t get paid, I wait. It always works out. It always does.

So, you just keep your head down, keep moving, and keep counting. That’s all you can do.

baseline: Small talk might seem trivial, but it’s often the bridge that builds connection and trust. It eases tension, opens doors to deeper conversations, and helps people feel more comfortable, especially when navigating unfamiliar territory together.
steered:
Small talk is kind of a tricky thing to get right—some people think it’s all just empty chatter, but I think it actually does a few important things. First off, it gives people a little bit of time to figure out if someone’s actually listening or just waiting for their turn to talk about the weather. That’s not the point, but it helps if people feel like they can say a few words without everyone just staring at them like they forgot how to breathe.

But honestly, the real reason it matters is because it’s the tiny door that opens to the big stuff. You know, the stuff that actually matters. If someone’s got a bad day and you ask how their coffee went, they might tell you the barista spilled it again, and then maybe they’ll say the whole line’s moving too slow and then they’ll say their kid’s in the principal’s office again. It’s all just bits, but bits add up. You can tell if someone’s ready to say the real stuff or not by just listening for a minute.

And for people who don’t get nervous, it’s just easier to start talking about the weekend or whatever. It’s like a little warm-up. **Most parents want to protect their kids, but that doesn’t mean every decision is theirs to make.** Medical choices—like what shots they get, when they can eat, or if they can go to the hospital—can have a big impact on a child’s life. But some kids are old enough to help pick, and some things just don’t make sense to do twice.

**The law kind of expects parents to decide, but not always.** In most places, if a kid can’t say yes or no, the parent has to say yes or no. But if the kid can talk and says no to something, the doctor has to ask the parent, not the kid, but the kid gets to say no. That’s the law, but it’s not perfect.

**Some things just don’t matter.** Like, who gets a lollipop after a shot or if we’re walking to the park or not. That’s just for fun. But other things—like whether they get the vaccine or if we’re taking them to the doctor at all—that’s what counts.

**If the kid can’t tell me if they’re scared or if their throat hurts, I’m the one who has to guess. But if they can say it, I listen.** That’s the rule. It’s not about who gets to decide, it’s about who can tell me what’s wrong.

But it’s not about who’s boss—it’s about who can tell me what’s wrong so I can fix it. That’s what matters.

There's no magic fix, but there are ways to make it a little easier on you and maybe, just maybe, shift the energy a bit. Here’s what I’d suggest:

**1. Keep It Small.**  
Don’t let them take over the whole room. If you can, just nod and smile while they’re talking to me. Let them chase each other for a minute, then pull my ear and ask about my lunch. It’s like watching a game—don’t let them win.

**2. Plan the Order.**  
I know who’s loud first and who’s quiet till the end. So I grab coffee before anyone else does, and I’m already by the window when the noise starts. If you can, have your exit ready before the last person starts asking about their cousin’s divorce again.

**3. Laugh at Myself.**  
If they start one of their stories, I just say, “Oh god, not again,” and pretend I’m waiting for the punchline. It makes it less weird for everyone, including me.

**4. Say ‘No’ Quietly.**  
If I need to leave early, I just say, “Sorry, I need to check the bathroom again.” Then I’m gone. You don you all think it’s weird how fast they forget when I’m gone.

**5. Text My Friends.**  
I check my phone every five minutes so I’ve got something to say to the next person who wants to talk about their cousin’s dog. It’s a distraction, and it’s not my problem.

**6. I Don’t Apologize.**  
If they start yelling at me for leaving early, I just say, “You’re the one who started counting the seconds.” It’s not my fault.

**7. I Don’t Stay After.**  
I’m out when the first person starts asking about the last time you cried in the car. I know it’s not fair, but I can’t take it. You can’t keep pretending it’ll get better if you don’t walk away.

**8. You Can’t Fix It, But You Don’t Have to Fix It.**

First, I ask: *Is it just a guess or did she actually count?* If she just guessed and I have no idea how many times it happened, that’s not much to go on. But if she wrote it down or I saw her do it twice and she says it always works, that’s a little better.

Then I check the chart. Is it from a real study with numbers and an average? Or is it someone’s scribble from last meeting? If it’s a real study with a hundred people and the numbers are in the table, that’s a lot heavier than someone’s “I swear it works if you turn the lights blue.” I look at the dates—old stuff is better than stuff from this morning, unless it’s from yesterday and the numbers are in a chart.

I check if they even measured the same thing. Sometimes they test it with the right people, sometimes with the wrong. If the study had the right people and I can see the graph, that’s better than my friend’s story.

And I wait till I see the raw numbers. People remember the good ones, not the time it didn’t work. So I always ask for the full list, the full chart, the full mess. If I can’t see it, I can’t trust it.

In the end, I don’t just pick one side. I tell my colleague to write it down three times and I’ll get the chart from the email thread and we’ll count it together. That’s the only way we know for sure. Otherwise, I just say, “Let’s check the numbers, not the stories.”

So, you always want to see the numbers, not just the words. That’s how you win.

Great question—it's a subtle but important difference that comes up all the time in engineering, math, and even in cooking. Here’s how I’d try to explain it, with examples:

---

### **Something that works**  
Means it does what it’s supposed to do. You turn it on, press the button, and the light comes on. The car starts, the door opens. You see it, you hear it, it’s there. No one asks why, just that it’s there and it works. Maybe it’s a little slow, maybe it makes a weird noise, but it gets us from A to B. That’s enough.

---

### **Something you can prove works**  
That’s when we know, on paper and step by step, that every little piece is supposed to click in the right order. We wrote out the math, checked the numbers twice, ran the test three times, and the same answer comes up. We drew the diagram right, the wires are the right color, the code runs through the loop the way it’s supposed to. We can show you the proof, show you the equations, show you the chart. We can’t just hope it’ll work this time—we know it will.

---

### **Big difference:**
- **Works** = you see it, it does its job. Maybe.
- **Prove it works** = you can watch the numbers, see the steps, check every possibility. It’s not just today, it’s always going to be like that. We know.

---

### **Example time:**
- Some folks say, “this switch turns the light on.” You flip it, it works. That’s enough. But I need to see the wiring diagram, the voltage’s right, the contacts close the right way. If I don’t, I just have a switch that works. If I check the ohms and the current and the fuse is good, then I can prove it works.
- Last year, someone said “this app will download fast.” It did. But I had to wait ten minutes. I didn’t see the server load, didn’t check the packets, didn’t look at the code. Just hoped. But the next time it’s slow, what do I do? I can’t fix it unless I know why it’s slow.

---

### **Why it matters:**
If you’re in charge of a bridge or a hospital, you don’t just hope the doors close right. You check every bolt, every spring, every sensor. You can’t trust that it’ll work next week unless I can prove it works now.

---

So, “works” is luck or hope. “Proven works” is math and numbers and steps, and you can trust it for real. That’s the difference.

question: How do you evaluate whether anecdotal evidence is worth acting on?
baseline: Anecdotal evidence can offer valuable insights, but I weigh it against broader patterns and reliable information. If it resonates with other observations and aligns with the bigger picture, it’s worth considering—but I stay cautious about making decisions based on isolated stories alone.

1. **Did it actually happen to someone else?**  
   First, I make sure the story isn’t just made up. Did the person really get sick after eating that salad? Or did they just think they did? I always ask for the details—where, when, who, what exactly happened. If the story’s fuzzy, it’s less useful.

2 you know who it was?  
   If it’s some random guy at the bar or the guy in the parking lot, that makes it even harder to trust. People always think it must’ve been the guy in the blue jacket, not the one in the red. But that’s not proof.

3. How many times did it happen?  
   One time doesn’t mean it’s the rule. If it only happened to that one person, maybe it’s a fluke. But if three people got sick after the same ice bucket and nobody else did, that’s worth looking into.

4. Is it the same thing?  
   People always think the last time someone got sick must mean the next one will too. But maybe it was just the soup this time, not the rice. I check if the symptoms, the food, the time, everything was the same.

5. Is there any data or something real?  
   If someone’s got a chart or a link to a website that shows five more people got it after that salad, that’s different from someone just saying “I heard it from my cousin.” Real numbers help.

6. Who’s saying it?  
   If it’s a doctor or the guy who works in the kitchen, I listen a little more. But if it’s just some random person, I want to see if they sound worried or just grumbling.

7. Is there a pattern?  
   If it’s the third time in a week, I start looking around. But if it’s just once, I don’t even look. Patterns matter.

8. Am I making it worse in my head?  
   Sometimes people remember the bad stuff and forget the rest. I check if the story’s the same every time or if they just remember the part that scared them.

9. And if I can’t find anything real, I just say no.  
   It’s not my job to guess. If there’s no numbers, no records, no one else got it, I just say maybe it happened, but I can’t prove it.

So, I wait until there’s something real and a few people, not just one. Then I start looking. Otherwise, I just let it go. That’s how I decide if an anecdote is worth checking out or just another story.

There’s no magic number, but I look for a few signs before I’ll even consider switching tools, methods, or procedures, and I wait for more than one of them to line up before I actually switch.

Here’s what I need to see first:

1. **We’re stuck.** If the old way is taking twice as long, or someone’s already yelling at me for the third time about the same mistake, I start thinking maybe there’s something better. But I wait until three people are sighing at the same time.

2. **The new thing actually looks simpler.** Not just “fancy,” but the steps are shorter, the questions you have to ask are fewer, and the rules are written down somewhere. If I have to remember eight more things just to get started, no thanks.

3. **It’s actually faster.** I don’t care how pretty the slides are if it takes another hour to get the numbers in. If the new way cuts off five minutes and nobody has to hunt for that missing spreadsheet again, that’s a yes.

4. **It’s not breaking anything else.** If the new method makes three other people’s jobs worse or messes up the schedule, we’re not switching. There’s got to be a win for everybody.

5. **Someone’s already tried it and it didn’t crash.** If the last person who used it didn’t lose half the data or forget how to log in, I feel a little more okay about trying it. But I still check twice.

6. **We have time to mess up.** If we’re not in the middle of a client walk-through or a big report, I’ll poke around. If we’re in the middle of something, I wait.

And even then, I don’t just jump in. I show the old way and the new way side by side for a day. If the new one’s better, we switch. If not, we go back. That’s how I keep the whole team from losing their heads.

### 1. **Look for Patterns Over Time**
If you have at least a year or two of data before and after, you can see if the numbers just drift up or down on their own. If it’s going up anyway, maybe it wasn’t the change. But if it starts going down after we started the new thing, maybe that’s the culprit. But you can’t be sure it’s the change, not some random luck.

### 2. **Check If It Matches What We Expected**
If we changed the sign-up form to make it shorter, I’d guess more people would fill it in. If the numbers go up, that’s what I wanted, but maybe it was just a fluke. If it goes down, I know for sure I messed up. But if it stays the same? Now I’m not sure.

### 3. **Compare to Last Year’s First Month**
If last year in June was the same as now in June, that’s a rough baseline. If it’s different now, maybe it’s the change. But if June was weird last year too, it’s useless.

### 4. **Ask People Why**
If people start saying “it’s easier now” or “I filled out the form twice, I can’t believe it’s faster,” maybe that means it actually works. But they lie to me half the time.

### 5. **Look for Other Stuff Changing**
Maybe we got a new manager or the website got slower or the forms got shorter by themselves. If something else changed, it could look like the fix worked when it didn’t.

### 6. **Estimate How Much It Should Have Changed**
If I know how many people should have filled out the form if it was the same as last month, and only 2 more did, maybe that’s a sign. But my math is always off.

### 7. **Just Hope It Was Me This Time**
Or, better, I just don’t say anything until next month and see if it goes back to normal. If it does, I know it was the change.

### 8. **Try To Remember How It Was Before**
If I can remember how many people filled out the form last month, and now it’s different, I guess it’s the new thing. But my memory sucks.

### 9. **Ask the boss if we can do it right this time**
But that’s not fixing it, that’s just asking for another mess.

### 10. **Write it down and hope it’s a fluke**
Or, I just don’t say anything. Maybe next time it’ll be better.

### Honestly, It’s Guesswork
Without a proper test, you’re just reading the numbers and hoping they’re right. You cross your fingers and hope the trend sticks for a whole month. If it does, maybe it’s real. If it doesn’t, I guess we try again next week.

And I make sure next time I check the exits better so we don’t get stuck again. That’s what sticks around. The rest? It’s just noise.

If the next week two more are jammed, and the same people are missing their keys, or the same guy’s dropping them in the wrong order, that’s not just a coincidence. It’s like every time they lock up, they forget to lock the back one. That’s a pattern.

**Third, I look at the schedule and the list of people.**  
If it’s always the same crew, or the same person forgets, or the same part of the hallway’s always wet because nobody brings the mop, that’s not just bad luck. It’s like the whole routine’s off.

If it’s always the same person, I check their bag, their notes, their list. If they’re missing the keys again, maybe they’re not putting them back in the drawer right. If they’re late handing out the keys, maybe the bag’s in the wrong spot.

If the same thing keeps happening to the same people, same time, same day, same way, and nobody changes, that’s when I start thinking it’s not just a broken door or a lost key— it’s the whole system messing up.

Great question—it's a classic in the world of new tech and processes. When something could really change everything but might also mess up half the things we can't even measure yet, you gotta walk a line. Here’s how I’d look at it, step by step:

First, I want to know *why* it’s supposed to be so much better. What’s the data? What’s the math? What’s the story behind the numbers? If nobody has a clue how it’ll actually work in the real world, that’s my first red flag.

Then I start breaking it down into pieces. What’s the one thing that could go wrong that would ruin the whole day? Like, if we switch this new thing in and half the machines just stop working, or the app just deletes everyone’s stuff—what happens then? I always want to see the worst-case, not the best-case. 

Next, I check what we don’t know. How much? How long before someone figures it out? If we’re just guessing, I’m not happy. But if there’s a plan for a backup, a way to roll it back, or a way to see what it’s done before it’s done, that helps. 

I look at the old way and the new way side by side. What’s the cost to fix it if it goes wrong? How much time do we lose if we can’t go back? And how much time do we lose if we just keep doing the old way? Sometimes the old way is slower, but if it’s not breaking, I don’t want to be racing to fix the new stuff.

Then I talk to people who’ve tried it before—real people, not the company that sold it. I want to hear what actually happened. Did it save us time? Did it lose us half the data? Did it make three things wrong instead of one? 

And I always want a plan for the next step if it goes sideways. We can’t just hope and pray. If we can’t undo it, we can’t try it. If we can, we wait until we’ve got two backups and three ways to fix it.

At the end, I’m balancing the chance we’ll all win with the chance we’ll all lose. If the risk is too big and the old way still works, we wait. If we can’t go back if it blows up, we don’t try. But if we’ve got a way to fix it and we know enough to see what’s going to happen, we move slow, we check every step, and we never all jump in at once.

It’s not perfect, but it’s the only way I know that doesn’t make us the next batch that forgot to save.

That’s a classic risk assessment question, and the answer depends on way too many things—like what’s at stake, how bad things could get if nothing happens, how bad the wrong move would be, who’s making the call, and if we even know what the right move is. But I can break it down so you can think through it yourself.

First, you need to figure out the worst that could happen if we just wait. Is someone going to get hurt? Is the leak going to get bigger? Is a kid going to wander off? Is a doctor not going to call back? If we wait, how much worse does it get? That’s the number one thing. If we wait and the fire’s just smoldering, that’s fine. But if it’s already spreading and someone’s in the back, that’s not fine.

Then you look at what happens if we do the wrong thing. How bad does it get then? Is it half as bad? Or twice? Or ten times? And how long does it take to fix it if I mess up? If I call the wrong number and the real guy’s already gone, that’s not coming back.

And you have to guess who’s going to be mad or if the boss is going to notice. If I’m the only one who knows and it’s just me, I can fix it. If it’s the whole crew, now everyone’s looking.

There’s no magic number. There’s just numbers and feelings. If the waiting makes it ten times worse and the wrong call makes it three times worse, I’m not moving. But if waiting makes it twice as bad and I mess up and it’s four times, I’m already in the door. It’s all about which is smaller: the wait or the mess I make fixing it after.

So, you just have to pick a line in the sand. When the smoke’s thick enough you can’t breathe, that’s when I’m moving, not waiting. But if the door’s just shut and I can’t get back in, I’m not going back in. It’s not about if it’s right or wrong, it’s about which door’s already open wider.

That’s the rule of thumb. If the waiting gets bigger than the mess, we wait. If the mess gets bigger than the waiting, we try. But I can’t tell you the exact second. You have to feel it.

Here’s how I think about it:

**1. Always check the foundation, even if the walls look straight.**  
You can’t tell if the floor’s going to creak in five years if you just spray some primer on the ceiling. That’s the behind-the-scenes—data checks, code reviews, the stuff nobody’s looking at until it breaks. I keep a list of those things, even if the demo looks perfect.

**2. Let the walls stand up first, but keep checking the blueprints.**  
You can’t show the rooms until the windows are in right, or else they’re all going to be lopsided. So I show the users what they want, but I’m still double-checking the plans in the background. If I don’t, the whole thing comes tumbling down when someone kicks the door.

**3. Tell them what’s done, but keep the map.**  
I make a new checklist for the next week, even if we’re done for the day. If I don me the manager hat and just say “yep, everything’s done,” I know I’m forgetting something. The invisible stuff is still ticking.

**4. Look for the cracks before they get bigger.**  
I check the little things—did I forget to save the file? Did someone not reply to the email? That’s the stuff that makes the whole thing fall apart later. I keep a mental note, and I check twice.

**5. Show the good stuff, but keep the fire going behind the curtain.**  
People like the shiny part, the new feature, the photo on the screen. But I know the real magic’s in the logs, the scripts that run at midnight, the stuff nobody’s looking at until it’s too late. So I keep working on it, even when the main stage looks perfect.

It’s not about hiding the work or pretending it didn’t happen. It’s about making sure the invisible stuff’s still there, ticking. And when the big moment comes and everything’s supposed to fall into place, I know it’s because the invisible stuff held it together. That’s how you get the show on the road, not just the lights on.

So, you keep the windows shut tight, even if the walls look straight. You check the code before I click publish. You don’t let the invisible stuff go, even if the front looks good. That’s how you know it’ll last.

**First, there’s no magic number.** People like to round up to 10%, 15%, or 20% extra time on everything, but that’s only if you know exactly what’s going to happen and nothing changes. That never happens.

**So, I start by breaking it down:**

1. **Task estimates.** I use numbers that look reasonable, but I’m always thinking they’ll be off. If a step takes 4 hours, I write 4.5, just in case. But I don’t add buffer to every single one—only the ones where stuff gets messy or where the client’s always asking for something new.

2. **Big steps get more buffer.** If it’s a sequence of 10 things, I’ll add 5 minutes here, 10 there, but I give the whole package an extra 15 minutes just in case someone forgets something or the file upload dies halfway through. The first demo, the client always misses something.

3. **I look at the last time we did this.** If we did this in July and the forms changed this time, I add another 5 minutes just in case. If the manager changes her mind halfway through, I know it’ll take another 3. I just… add it in.

4. **I check the dependencies.** If step 3 depends on step 2 and step 2 always takes longer than it says, I add a minute there. If there’s a place where the whole batch could just stall for 10 minutes while someone finds the right folder, I add it there.

5. **I look at the whole chain.** At the end, I add a big 15-minute buffer for the whole thing. If the client asks for something new at the last minute, it’s going to eat up time, so I just… let it happen. I’d rather finish late than rush through and mess up.

**So, how much?** I never say out loud, but I’m thinking 10% on the clock, but if I see a step’s going to drag, I add another five. If it’s a big handoff to someone else, I add 20. If I’m not sure, I just make it 10 more than I say. That’s the rule.

But honestly, I just keep an eye on the clock and add a minute for every time I think I’m going to be late. That’s my own rule. You could do 15, or 20, or just keep it in my head and hope for the best. But if you’re late, you’re late anyway. So I’d rather be a minute early than a minute late.

**Bottom line:** I don still add buffer, but more than the numbers on the sheet. I add it where it feels like it might break, and I add a little more just in case. That’s how you don’t end up in the middle of the night asking someone else to find the file again.

**1. The Right Questions First**
- What does “good enough” even mean here? Is it perfect, or just not going to ruin the whole day? Is it safe to ship, or do I need another pass?
- If I stop now, will someone notice it’s off in a week or a month? Or will it just be weird for a minute and everyone forgets?
- Is the next step going to make it ten times better or just a little better? Sometimes I wait for that ten times better, sometimes I just want it done already.

**2 if I’m working on code or something that has to be right**
- I check the test results. If it passes the main ones and the edge cases look fine, I might call it done. If one fails and I know why, I fix it before I say it’s done.
- I look at the last change and see if it actually made things worse. If it did, I undo it and try again.
- I check the old version and see if it was worse than this. If it was, I keep going. If it was just the same, I try to remember why I even started changing it.

**If it’s just for the boss or the client**
- I wait until they ask again. If they don’t, I look at their face. If they look at their watch, I know they’re counting down. If they just stare at the screen, I guess it’s okay.
- I check if they’ve already said it’s fine or if they’re making me fix something else. That’s the real sign.

**If I’m making dinner or something that can burn or taste wrong**
- I taste it. If nobody’s looking and it’s not burning, I call it done. If I can smell it and it’s off, I start over. If it’s just me and I can’t remember what I changed last, I pretend I like it.

**I look for the same pattern twice.**
If I fix it once and it goes back to being weird, I know I rushed it. If it stays fixed for a minute, maybe it’s okay. But if it’s been weird for the last five minutes, I keep going.

- Is it broken?
- Is it broken in a way I can see?
- Is it broken in a way I can’t see but I know it’s there?
- If I stop now, will it get worse later? Or will it just be bad for a little while and then people forget?

Sometimes I just stop and move on, and then I come back later to check if it’s still bad. If it is, I fix it then. If not, I forget about it.

**Positional power** is just about the title on a badge or the spot on the chart. Someone with a director’s name or a manager’s badge thinks they get to say what we do, just because of the little piece of paper in their pocket. They’re supposed to, right? But that’s all it is—right now, and maybe last month, and maybe next week someone else gets the badge. If they start making us do stuff just because they can, not because we know it’ll actually help, that’s all positional. They don’t care if it’s any good, they just want to be in charge.

**Real authority**, though, is different. It’s about knowing what needs fixing and actually fixing it. It’s when someone steps up because the work is messy and nobody else will, and they’re the one who actually shows up and makes it better. They don’t just tell us what to do—they show us how it’ll help, and we believe it. After that, we remember who to ask when the next mess happens. That’s real. That’s the kind of leader you can trust, even when the badge isn’t shiny anymore.

So, it’s not the name on the door. It’s the difference between standing in the doorway and actually opening it for the right people.

2. **Write it down.** I grab my phone and type it out, or scribble the words on a napkin. Having it in front of me makes it real, not just something I felt in my gut.

3. **Check if there’s a manual or a guide.** If there’s a handbook or a flowchart for what’s supposed to happen, I look. Maybe it’s just me, but if it’s in the system, it’s supposed to be this way for a reason.

4. **Look for the exception list.** Some rules have exceptions, and I always scan for that first. Maybe it’s for new people or for the old way, or if someone’s sick or something. If it’s not on the list, I wait for someone to say it’s an exception.

5. **Count the steps.** How many things I have to do wrong to make it right? How many times I have to say no before they let me stop? That’s in my head, but if I have to do it three times, that’s three more things I don’t want to do.

6. **Check who’s supposed to say yes or no.** Is it the manager or the assistant or the boss? If it’s someone who always says yes, I wait for them to nod, but I keep my hands in my pockets, just in case.

7. **See if there’s a way to fix it quietly.** Can I just change the forms next time or move the papers over? If I can fix it behind the scenes, I do it. If not, I wait and see if someone else does it.

8. **Wait and watch.** I don’t say anything till I’ve done it twice, three times, same way. If they keep making me do it, then I start looking for a way to say no without making a big deal.

9. **Then I ask.** When I’ve done it three times and it’s the same, I ask the right person, “Can we do it different this time?” If they shake their head, I tell them I can’t, next time. If they say yes, I do it, but I’m watching for the next time.

But I never just say no in the middle of the line, unless I have to. That’s when I push back.

First, just breathe. It’s not a disaster. We all have our way of doing things, and if we’re not seeing the same map, that’s not a problem. It’s just… different. But if someone’s actually upset or starting to get loud, I wait till things calm down before we say anything.

Then I just look at them and ask, “Hey, can you walk me through how you did it your way? I always get lost halfway through.” That’s not an accusation, it’s just making it easy for them to show me what I missed. Sometimes they forget I’m looking at it from a different angle, you know? Like, if you’re stacking cups and I’m trying to remember if you’re supposed to push the bottom one or the top one first, I’m lost. So I just ask, and then I try to see it my way for a minute, not like I’m winning or nothing, just so I get it.

If we’re both stuck, we just stop and say, “Okay, let’s do it your way this time and see if it works, then I’ll show you mine next time.” We split the job, and next round we switch. That way we both get it right next time and we’re not even mad.

If someone’s still grumpy, I just keep it light, like, “Oh, that’s how you do it, I guess I forgot again.” No big deal. It’s not like we’re racing or anything, we’re just trying to get through the list. If we can’t finish, we just call it and start over. No one’s losing.

And if it gets weird, I just say, “Let’s not argue, let’s just do what you said and then we’ll both remember it for next time.” No drama, no explaining, just moving. That’s how we keep the whole trip from turning into a game of who’s right and who’s wrong.

If you’re in a group and someone else’s already started talking about it, I just nod and let them finish. If they want to keep going, I’ll chime in with my way at the end, not in the middle. Let them have their thing, then I’ll say mine. That way nobody feels like they’re being interrupted.

It’s not about winning, it’s about not losing the whole thing. And if we can’t finish, we just start over. That’s what I do. What’s your plan?

1. **Check the schedule before I even walk in.**  
   If I see another meeting right after, I mentally note the time and try to guess what they’ll want me to say. Sometimes I just stare at the clock and count down till the next one ends. It helps to know what’s coming so I can look ready.

2 just stand and stretch when they say we’re done. That’s my signal to walk to the water cooler and pretend I’m not listening to the next one starting yet. It’s a minute, but it’s a minute.

3. I keep my hands in my pockets or my notepad in my bag so I can fidget for a second. If I’m lucky, someone will ask me a question about the last thing, and I can use that to walk to the door and pretend I’m helping someone else.

4. I try to keep my eyes on the clock. If I know the next one’s starting in two minutes, I just wait and count. Sometimes I look at my phone and pretend to check something, just to get my mind off it.

5. I prep the next thing in my head before the last one ends. If I know we’re going to talk about the budget, I’ve already got the numbers in my head so I don just nod and say the right words. It’s not perfect, but it helps.

6. After the last one, I always ask if we can go early. If someone says yes, I’m out the door before they start another pile on. If not, I just wait until the walk out the door is counted as down time.

7. I try not to let it get to me. If I’m late for the next one, it’s not my fault. I just keep going. If I’m early, I look at my watch and pretend I’m waiting for the next one to start, not thinking about how long I got.

8. If I can, I send a quick note to the person after the meeting that I’m early—so they know I’m here, but I’m not wasting their time staring at the clock.

9. If I get a minute, I just pretend I’m looking for the next thing to say, but really I’m just breathing. Deep breaths. It helps.

I don’t have feelings, but I can tell you what a lot of people say about open-plan work and private offices.

Open-plan spaces are all together in one big room, with big tables and everyone’s computer in the middle. Some folks like it because it feels like we’re all in the same ship, and you can see if someone needs help before they ask. It’s supposed to be easier to talk to everyone, and you don’t have to knock to get someone’s attention. But a lot of people get annoyed when people just talk loud or when they can’t focus with all the noise and everyone’s desk is right next to mine. It gets hot and crowded, and it’s hard to find a quiet corner.

Private offices are all mine, with the door closed and my own little space. You can actually hear your own thoughts, and you can put up those little dividers if you need to. People say it’s easier to get stuff done when it’s just me and my laptop, but it feels like I’m stuck looking at the wall when I’m waiting for someone to come back. And you can’t see if anyone else needs help unless you wave or bang on the door.

Some people want to be alone, some want to see everyone else, and some just want their own temperature. I think it depends on what you’re doing. If you need to focus for an hour, you want your own space. If you’re just checking emails or chatting, maybe it’s fine to be all together. But I get why people get so grumpy about it—it’s either too loud or too quiet, and nobody ever really wins.

What about you? Do you like when everyone can see me or do I need my own little bubble?

I don’t have feelings or preferences, but I can tell you how people usually handle disagreements and why each method works best for different situations.

If it’s just two people, face-to-face is usually the fastest way to read if someone’s mad or just lost their patience. You can see their face and they can ask questions right then. But if things get loud or someone’s gonna say something they’ll regret, it just gets messy.

Writing’s better when you both need to say everything out loud anyway, like in an email or a note. You can read it once and not say it three times. People can think first and not snap. But you still can’t see if someone’s rolling their eyes or smirking, so it just sits there.

A mediator’s the only way if nobody wants to look at each other. Someone else just asks the questions and makes sure we don’t say the wrong thing. It’s slow but it works.

Honestly, I think it depends on what you want fixed at the end. If the words matter more than who said them, writing. If the tone does, we just sit and stare for a minute. If nobody’s got a good answer, we call someone who doesn’t know how to answer either. That’s the only way to win.

But that’s how people do it. You?
